title: Concept Drift Detection: Insights from a Comprehensive Benchmark Framework
authors: Cerqueira, V.; Torgo, L.; Soares, C.
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
tldr: Introduces a benchmark framework for evaluating concept drift detectors, finding that DDM performs best overall while ADWIN excels in noisy data.
problem_and_motivation: Concept drift, where data distribution changes over time, is a critical challenge in stream mining. While many drift detectors exist, there is no comprehensive benchmark framework to evaluate them systematically. Existing evaluations often use ad-hoc experimental setups that make it difficult to compare methods fairly. The paper addresses the need for a standardized, reproducible benchmark that considers multiple drift types, noise levels, and evaluation metrics.
approach: Developed a benchmark framework with 4,200 synthetic datasets covering 14 drift types, 10 noise levels, and 30 random seeds.
Generated drift datasets using ADAPT library with controlled parameters for abrupt, gradual, incremental, and recurring drift.
Applied 6 concept drift detection methods: DDM, ADWIN, EDDM, HDDM_A, HDDM_W, and PageHinkley.
Used multiple evaluation metrics: time to detection (TTD), time to recovery (TTR), false positive rate (FPR), and false negative rate (FNR).
Conducted statistical analysis using Friedman test and Nemenyi post-hoc test for significance comparison.
Tested both univariate and multivariate data generation scenarios.
findings: DDM achieves the best overall performance across most metrics and drift types.
ADWIN performs best for noisy data due to its adaptive windowing approach.
EDDM excels at detecting gradual drifts but has higher false positive rates.
PageHinkley is effective for detecting abrupt changes but performs poorly on gradual drifts.
No single detector dominates across all scenarios — method selection should consider specific data characteristics.
Noise level significantly affects detector performance, with most methods degrading as noise increases.
Gradual and incremental drifts are harder to detect than abrupt drifts for all methods.

key_equations.explanation: Time to Detection: the delay between when a concept change occurs (tc) and when the detector signals it (td).
Time to Recovery: the time between detector signal and return to normal error rates.
False Positive Rate: proportion of normal instances incorrectly flagged as drift.
False Negative Rate: proportion of drift instances that go undetected.

definitions.definition: Changes in the underlying data distribution over time that can degrade model performance in stream mining applications.
Sudden, immediate change in data distribution that occurs instantaneously.
Slow transition from one concept to another over a period of time.
Continuous, progressive change in data distribution over time.
Drift that appears and disappears periodically, with concepts repeating over time.
A drift detection method that monitors error rate and triggers alarms when statistical properties change significantly.
A drift detection method that maintains a variable-length window of recent observations and detects changes by comparing subwindows.
An extension of DDM that focuses on the distance between errors rather than error rate, enabling earlier drift detection.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper introduces a comprehensive benchmark framework for evaluating concept drift detectors, addressing the lack of standardized evaluation in stream mining. By systematically testing 6 detectors across 4,200 synthetic datasets with controlled drift types and noise levels, it provides actionable insights for method selection. The finding that DDM performs best overall while ADWIN excels in noisy conditions helps practitioners choose appropriate detectors based on their data characteristics. The framework enables reproducible comparisons and can be extended to evaluate new drift detection methods.

ADWIN is the best choice for noisy data due to adaptive windowing.
Gradual and incremental drifts are significantly harder to detect than abrupt drifts.

The benchmark framework covers 14 drift types, 10 noise levels, and 30 random seeds.
